hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
Harness Engineering 2.0 is here!

We benchmark models all the time but the harness running the model can dramatically improve the result, cost, and execution time too.

And finally, devs just open-sourced Harness Arena, where you can test the same task across multiple harness and model combinations side by side.

You provide one task and then run it across several model x harness configs that you want to test.

Every config receives the same prompt, files, tools, skills, and evaluation checks. Harness Arena then returns:

- total cost
- execution time
- whether the task passed
- files and artifacts produced

If you want to try it yourself, it is implemented within the open-source HarnessRouter project.

Here's the repo: https://t.co/4y6zJShKSu

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

HarnessRouter is a plug-and-play infrastructure layer that lets you run any harness under a single interface, like:

- Codex
- Hermes
- Claude code
- DeepSeek Harness
- System One, powered by Jev
- And 25 more agent harnesses

In Harness Arena, the cheapest run does not automatically win.

A config must complete the task correctly first. Cost and execution time are compared only among the configurations that pass.

Here's the result from one Harness Arena test:

- Hermes + GPT-5.2: 5/5 successful runs using 0.47 credits
- Claude Code + Opus 4.8: 3/5 successful runs using 223 credits

That is around 474x difference in credits, while the more expensive configuration also failed two runs.

You can keep the model fixed to measure how much the harness changes the result. Or vary both to find the best harness and model pairing for that task.

This helps answer practical questions such as:

- Should this task run on Codex or Claude?
- Can a cheaper config still pass every check?
- Which setup is best to handle this workload?

Once you find the best config, you can run future tasks through it using the same Unified Harness Protocol (UHP) interface for sessions, streaming, files, artifacts, cancellation, and failures.

So you are no longer choosing an agent stack based only on a model leaderboard.

Instead, you can benchmark the complete runtime on the task your product actually needs to solve.

To dive deeper, my co-founder wrote an article explaining why model routing is different from harness routing, how UHP works, and what supporting multiple agent runtimes involves.

It also covers the local setup, a working request, and how sessions and files move through the system.

Read it below.

hits.name: Shubham Saboo
hits.text:
Memory in AI Agent Harness.

LLMs are stateless, so every bit of memory in an AI agent is something the harness saves to disk and loads back in when it needs it.

most good agent harnesses split that memory into a few layers, let's look at each one of them: 

• context: what the model can see in the current session. when it gets close to full, the harness summarizes the older messages to make room.

• notes: a progress file the agent keeps updating while it works, so if a session ends halfway the next one can read it and continue from there.

• semantic: facts about you, your team and your project, like your preferences or which repo you work in. Hermes keeps these in MEMORY.md and USER.md.

• procedural: how to do a specific job. when the agent figures out something hard, it writes it down as a skill and uses that skill the next time.

• episodic: a log of every past session that the agent can search when it needs to remember what happened before.

First two only last as long as the session or the task. Other three are persistent, so they're still there the next time you start the agent.

save this for the next time someone asks how agents remember.

We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

outsiders.name: Anthropic
outsiders.text:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).

outsiders.name: Anthropic
outsiders.text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8
